label: def:weak-solution
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:weak-solution}
Let $\{u(t,x):t\in[0,T],\ x\in\mathbb R\}$ be a real-valued adapted
stochastic process such that, for every $t\in[0,T]$ and $x\in\mathbb R$,
$$
G_{t-s}(x-y)\sigma(u(s,y))\mathbf{1}_{[0,t]}(s)
$$
is integrable with respect to $W$.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] We say that $u$ is a
\emph{mild solution} to \eqref{eq:SHE} if, for every
$t\in[0,T]$ and $x\in\mathbb R$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq solution nonlinear}
u(t,x)
=
(G_t*u_0)(x)
+
\int_0^t\int_\mathbb R
G_{t-s}(x-y)\sigma(u(s,y))\,W(\mathrm d s,\mathrm d y) \ \ \ \  \text{a.s.}
\end{equation}
\item[(ii)]
We say that \eqref{eq:SHE} admits a \emph{weak solution} on $[0,T]$
if there exists a complete filtered probability space
$$
\left(\widetilde{\Omega},\widetilde{\mathcal F},
(\widetilde{\mathcal F}_t)_{t\ge0},\widetilde{\mathbb P}\right)
$$
satisfying the usual conditions and carrying an initial field
$\widetilde u_0$, a Gaussian random field $\widetilde W$,
and an $(\widetilde{\mathcal F}_t)_{t\ge0}$-adapted random field
$$
\{\widetilde u(t,x):t\in[0,T],\ x\in\mathbb R\}
$$
 
with the following properties.
The initial field $\widetilde u_0$ is
$\widetilde{\mathcal F}_0\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$-measurable,
and its law as an $L^{q_0}_\lambda(\mathbb R)$-valued random variable
coincides with that of $u_0$.
The noise $\widetilde W$ has the same law as $W$,
and its associated $\mathcal H$-cylindrical process is a Wiener process
with respect to $(\widetilde{\mathcal F}_t)_{t\ge0}$.
Finally, $\widetilde u$ is a mild solution to \eqref{eq:SHE}
with initial datum $\widetilde u_0$ and driving noise $\widetilde W$.
\end{itemize}

title: Proof
body_md:
Part (i) follows from the proof of
\cite[Lemma~2.5]{HW2022}.

For (ii), we first consider deterministic $f$ and put
$q'=q/(q-1)$. 
By H\"older's inequality and (i), we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\int_\mathbb R
|\partial_x^jG_t(x-y)|\,|f(y)|\mathrm d y\\
\le&\,
\left\|f\right\|_{L^q_\lambda}
\left(
\int_\mathbb R
|\partial_x^jG_t(z)|^{q'}
\lambda(x-z)^{-q'/q}\mathrm d z
\right)^{1/q'}\\
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-1/q}\left\|f\right\|_{L^q_\lambda}
\left(
\int_\mathbb R
|\partial_x^jG_t(z)|^{q'}
(1+|z|)^{2(1-H)q'/q}\mathrm d z
\right)^{1/q'}\\
\le&\,
C_{T_0,T,q,H,j}
\lambda(x)^{-1/q}\left\|f\right\|_{L^q_\lambda},
\end{aligned}
$$
where the last inequality follows from the uniform Gaussian
decay of the heat-kernel derivatives for $t\in[T_0,T]$.

 For each fixed $x\in\mathbb R$, the Gaussian bounds give
$$
\sup_{\substack{t\in[T_0,T]\\ |a|\le1}}
|\partial_x^mG_t(x+a-y)|
\le C e^{-c|x-y|^2},
\qquad 0\le m\le j.
$$
Since $e^{-c|x-y|^2}|f(y)|$ is integrable, we may differentiate
the convolution by differentiating the heat kernel inside the
integral. The preceding estimate then proves \eqref{eq:msmooth}
for deterministic $f$. 
 

For random $f\in L^q_\lambda(\Omega\times\mathbb R)$, we have
$f(\omega,\cdot)\in L^q_\lambda(\mathbb R)$ almost surely.
Applying the preceding estimate pathwise and using $p\le q$,
we obtain
$$
\begin{aligned}
\left\|\partial_x^j(G_t*f)(x)\right\|_p
&\le
C\lambda(x)^{-1/q}
\left\|\left\|f\right\|_{L^q_\lambda(\mathbb R)}\right\|_p\\
&\le
C\lambda(x)^{-1/q}
\left(\mathbb E\left\|f\right\|_{L^q_\lambda(\mathbb R)}^q\right)^{1/q}\\
&=
C\lambda(x)^{-1/q}
\left\|f\right\|_{L^q_\lambda(\Omega\times\mathbb R)}.
\end{aligned}
$$
This proves \eqref{eq:msmooth}.

label: lem:semigroup-fubini
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:semigroup-fubini}
Fix $r_0>0$ and $q_H<q\le q_0$, and let $k$ be
a Schwartz function on $\mathbb R$. Then, for every fixed $x\in\mathbb R$,
we have almost surely
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\int_\mathbb R k(z)
\bigl[u(r_0,x-z)-(G_{r_0}*u_0)(x-z)\bigr]\mathrm d z\\
 =&\, 
\int_0^{r_0}\int_\mathbb R
(k*G_{r_0-s})(x-y)\sigma(u(s,y))W(\mathrm d s,\mathrm d y).
\end{aligned}
$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $x\in\mathbb R$.
By \eqref{eq:umom} and Lemma~\ref{lem:initial-smoothing}(ii),
$$
\left\|u(r_0,x-z)-(G_{r_0}*u_0)(x-z)\right\|_2\le C\lambda(x-z)^{-1/q}.
$$
Using \eqref{eq:stochastic-isometry}, \eqref{eq solution nonlinear},  
and  
Lemma~\ref{lem:initial-smoothing}(i), we have 
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\int_\mathbb R |k(z)|
\left(
\mathbb E\int_0^{r_0}
\left\|
G_{r_0-s}(x-z-\cdot)\sigma(u(s,\cdot))
\right\|_{\mathcal H}^2\mathrm d s
\right)^{1/2}\mathrm d z\\
 = &\,
\int_\mathbb R |k(z)|\left\|u(r_0,x-z)-(G_{r_0}*u_0)(x-z)\right\|_2\mathrm d z\\
 \le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-1/q}
\int_\mathbb R |k(z)|(1+|z|)^{2(1-H)/q}\mathrm d z
<\infty,
\end{aligned}
$$
where finiteness follows from the rapid decay of $k$.
Thus the convolution on the left-hand side
is well defined in $L^2(\Omega)$, and stochastic Fubini's theorem
yields the stated identity.

label: eq:initial-sharp
title: Proof
body_md:
It suffices to prove the estimates for $2\le p\le q$,
since the bounds for lower moments then follow from Jensen's inequality.
Fix $s,t\in[T_0,T]$ and $x,y\in\mathbb R$.
By symmetry, we may assume $s\le t$.
Splitting the stochastic convolution at time $T_0/2$, we write
\begin{equation}\label{eq:initial-sharp}
u(t,x)=(G_t*u_0)(x)+I(t,x)+J(t,x),
\end{equation}
where
$$
\begin{aligned}
I(t,x):=&\,
\int_0^{T_0/2}\int_\mathbb R
G_{t-r}(x-z)\sigma(u(r,z))W(\mathrm d r,\mathrm d z),\\
J(t,x):=&\,
\int_{T_0/2}^t\int_\mathbb R
G_{t-r}(x-z)\sigma(u(r,z))W(\mathrm d r,\mathrm d z).
\end{aligned}
$$
We estimate the increments of these three terms separately.


Since $\partial_tG_t=\partial_x^2G_t$, the fundamental theorem
of calculus, Minkowski's inequality, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:initial-smoothing}(ii) yield
\begin{equation}\label{eq:initial-sharp-expanded}
\begin{aligned}
&\left\|(G_t*u_0)(x)-(G_s*u_0)(y)\right\|_p\\
\le&\,
\int_s^t
\left\|\partial_x^2(G_r*u_0)(x)\right\|_p\mathrm d r
+|x-y|\int_0^1
\left\|\partial_x(G_s*u_0)(y+\theta(x-y))\right\|_p\mathrm d\theta\\
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-1/q}|t-s|
+
C|x-y|\int_0^1
\lambda(y+\theta(x-y))^{-1/q}\mathrm d\theta\\
\le&\,
C\bigl(\lambda(x)^{-1/q}+\lambda(y)^{-1/q}\bigr)
\bigl(|t-s|+|x-y|\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

 

Set
$$
f(z):=u(T_0/2,z)-(G_{T_0/2}*u_0)(z).
$$
By Lemma~\ref{lem:semigroup-fubini},
$$
I(t,x)-I(s,y)
=
(G_{t-T_0/2}*f)(x)-(G_{s-T_0/2}*f)(y).
$$
Moreover, \eqref{eq:msmooth} and \eqref{eq:umom} imply
$$
\left\|f(z)\right\|_p\le C\lambda(z)^{-1/q},
\qquad z\in\mathbb R.
$$
By Minkowski's inequality, the preceding bound on $f$,
\eqref{eq:weight-ratio}, and the Gaussian decay of the
heat-kernel derivatives, we obtain
$$
\begin{aligned}
 \left\|(\partial_aG_a*f)(v)\right\|_p
+\left\|(G_a'*f)(v)\right\|_p 
\le&\,
\int_\mathbb R
\bigl(
|\partial_aG_a(v-z)|+|G_a'(v-z)|
\bigr)\left\|f(z)\right\|_p\,\mathrm d z\\
\le&\, C\lambda(v)^{-1/q},
\end{aligned}
$$
uniformly for $a\in[T_0/2,T]$ and $v\in\mathbb R$.
Here $G_a'$ denotes the spatial derivative of $G_a$.
Applying the fundamental theorem of calculus to the heat kernels,
as in \eqref{eq:initial-sharp-expanded}, yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:early-stochastic-sharp}
\left\|I(t,x)-I(s,y)\right\|_p
\le
C\bigl(\lambda(x)^{-1/q}+\lambda(y)^{-1/q}\bigr)
\bigl(|t-s|+|x-y|\bigr).
\end{equation}

For $t\in[T_0,T]$ and $0<|h|\le1$, applying
\eqref{eq:BDG-product} to the spatial increment of $J$ gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\left\|J(t,x+h)-J(t,x)\right\|_p^2\\
\le&\,
C\int_{T_0/2}^t\int_{\mathbb R^2}
|D_{t-r}(x-z-\eta,h)-D_{t-r}(x-z,h)|^2
\left\|\sigma(u(r,z))\right\|_p^2
|\eta|^{2H-2}\mathrm d z\mathrm d\eta\mathrm d r\\
&+C\int_{T_0/2}^t\int_\mathbb R
|D_{t-r}(x-z,h)|^2
\bigl[\mathcal N_{1/2-H,p}\sigma(u(r,\cdot))(z)\bigr]^2
\mathrm d z\mathrm d r.
\end{aligned}
$$
The Lipschitz continuity of $\sigma$, together with
\eqref{eq:umom} and \eqref{eq:ufrac}, yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sigma-bounds}
\left\|\sigma(u(r,z))\right\|_p
+
\mathcal N_{1/2-H,p}\sigma(u(r,\cdot))(z)
\le C\lambda(z)^{-1/q},
\end{equation}
uniformly for $r\in[T_0/2,T]$.

For $q>q_H$, write 
\begin{align}\label{eq a}
    a_q:=4(1-H)/q.
\end{align} 
Clearly,   $a_q<1-2H$.  Lemmas~\ref{lem:weightedenergy}
and \ref{lem:singleenergy}(i), together with
\eqref{eq:weight-ratio} and \eqref{eq:sigma-bounds}, yield
\begin{equation}\label{eq:J-space-sharp}
\left\|J(t,x+h)-J(t,x)\right\|_p^2
\le C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}\bigl(|h|^{2H}+|h|\bigr)
\le C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}|h|^{2H},
\end{equation}
where the last inequality uses $0<|h|\le1$ and $2H<1$.

To estimate the temporal increment of $J$, suppose $s<t$
and $t-s\le1$. Write
$$
J(t,x)-J(s,x)=A(x)+B(x),
$$
where
$$
\begin{aligned}
A(x):=&\,
\int_s^t\int_\mathbb R
G_{t-r}(x-z)\sigma(u(r,z))W(\mathrm d r,\mathrm d z),\\
B(x):=&\,
\int_{T_0/2}^s\int_\mathbb R
\bigl[G_{t-r}(x-z)-G_{s-r}(x-z)\bigr]
\sigma(u(r,z))W(\mathrm d r,\mathrm d z).
\end{aligned}
$$
Using \eqref{eq:BDG-product}, \eqref{eq:sigma-bounds},
\eqref{t:eq:kernel-L2}, and  \eqref{t:eq:kernel-weighted}
with $\vartheta=0$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:A-temporal}
\begin{aligned}
\left\|A(x)\right\|_p^2
\le&\,
C\int_s^t\int_{\mathbb R^2}
|D_{t-r}(x-z,h)|^2\lambda(z)^{-2/q}
|h|^{2H-2}\mathrm d z\mathrm d h\mathrm d r\\
&+C\int_s^t\int_\mathbb R
G_{t-r}(x-z)^2\lambda(z)^{-2/q}\mathrm d z\mathrm d r\\
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}\int_0^{t-s}
\bigl(r^{H-1}+r^{-1/2}\bigr)\mathrm d r\\
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}(t-s)^H.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Similarly, \eqref{eq:BDG-product} and \eqref{eq:sigma-bounds} yield
$$
\begin{aligned}
\left\|B(x)\right\|_p^2
\le&\,
C\int_{T_0/2}^s\int_{\mathbb R^2}
|D_{t-r}(x-z,h)-D_{s-r}(x-z,h)|^2
\lambda(z)^{-2/q}|h|^{2H-2}\mathrm d z\mathrm d h\mathrm d r\\
&+C\int_{T_0/2}^s\int_\mathbb R
|G_{t-r}(x-z)-G_{s-r}(x-z)|^2
\lambda(z)^{-2/q}\mathrm d z\mathrm d r.
\end{aligned}
$$
With $v=s-r$, the triangle inequality and the kernel estimates
\eqref{t:eq:kernel-L2}-\eqref{t:eq:kernel-time-H} give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:B-temporal}
\begin{aligned}
\left\|B(x)\right\|_p^2
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}\int_0^T
\bigl(v^{H-1}+v^{-1/2}\bigr)
\min\left\{1,\frac{(t-s)^2}{v^2}\right\}\mathrm d v\\
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}
\bigl((t-s)^H+(t-s)^{1/2}\bigr)\\
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}(t-s)^H,
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where the second inequality follows by splitting the integral
at $v=t-s$.

Combining \eqref{eq:A-temporal} and \eqref{eq:B-temporal} yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:J-time-sharp}
\left\|J(t,x)-J(s,x)\right\|_p
\le C\lambda(x)^{-1/q}|t-s|^{H/2}.
\end{equation}
Taking square roots in \eqref{eq:J-space-sharp} and using
\eqref{eq:J-time-sharp}, we obtain, for
$|t-s|\le1$ and $|x-y|\le1$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\left\|J(t,x)-J(s,y)\right\|_p
\le&\,
\left\|J(t,x)-J(s,x)\right\|_p
+\left\|J(s,x)-J(s,y)\right\|_p\\
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-1/q}|t-s|^{H/2}
+C\lambda(y)^{-1/q}|x-y|^H.
\end{aligned}
$$
Together with the decomposition \eqref{eq:initial-sharp}
and the estimates \eqref{eq:initial-sharp-expanded}
and \eqref{eq:early-stochastic-sharp}, this proves
\eqref{eq:exact-holder} in this case.
If either $|t-s|>1$ or $|x-y|>1$, the conclusion follows
directly from \eqref{eq:umom}.

label: t:lem:errors
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{t:lem:errors}
Let $q_H<q\le q_0$, $2\le p\le q/2$, and
$0<\vartheta<\vartheta_q$.
There exists a constant $C<\infty$ such that the following
estimates hold uniformly for $t\in[T_0,T]$, $x\in\mathbb R$,
and $0<\varepsilon<1$ with $\varepsilon^\beta<T_0/4$:
\begin{align}
\left\|J_1-\widetilde J_1\right\|_p
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-1/q}\varepsilon^{H/2+\vartheta},
\label{t:eq:J1-bound}\\
\left\|J_{2,\beta}\right\|_p
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-1/q}
\bigl(\varepsilon^{1+\beta(H/2-1)}+\varepsilon^{1/4}\bigr),
\label{t:eq:J2-bound}\\
\left\|J_{3,\beta}-\widetilde J_{3,\beta}\right\|_p
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-1/q}\varepsilon^{\beta(H/2+\vartheta)}.
\label{t:eq:refreeze-bound}
\end{align}

label: eq:N-seminorm-sigma
title: Proof
body_md:
The condition $0<\vartheta<\vartheta_q$ implies
$$
2\vartheta<H,
\qquad
a_q+4\vartheta<1-2H,
\qquad
H+2\vartheta<1/2.
$$
Here, $a_q$ is defined in \eqref{eq a}.
                                                                                                                                                             
By the Lipschitz continuity of $\sigma$ and \eqref{eq:ufrac},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:N-seminorm-sigma}
\mathcal N_{1/2-H,p}\sigma(u(s,\cdot))(y)
\le C\lambda(y)^{-1/q},
\qquad s\in[T_0/2,T+1].
\end{equation}

\noindent
\emph{Step 1.}
Set
$$
\xi_1(s,y):=\sigma(u(s,y))-\sigma(u(t,x)),
\qquad t<s\le t+\varepsilon.
$$
Since $\sigma(u(t,x))$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable,
$\xi_1$ is predictable on $(t,t+\varepsilon]$.
Moreover, the frozen value does not depend on $y$, so
\eqref{eq:N-seminorm-sigma} gives
$$
\mathcal N_{1/2-H,p}\xi_1(s,\cdot)(y)
=
\mathcal N_{1/2-H,p}\sigma(u(s,\cdot))(y)
\le C\lambda(y)^{-1/q}.
$$
By the Lipschitz continuity of $\sigma$, \eqref{eq:umom}, and
  \eqref{eq:exact-holder},  we have
$$
\left\|\xi_1(s,y)\right\|_p^2
\le
C\bigl(\lambda(y)^{-2/q}+\lambda(x)^{-2/q}\bigr)
\bigl((s-t)^{2\vartheta}+|x-y|^{4\vartheta}\bigr).
$$

Applying \eqref{eq:BDG-product}, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:J1-error-decomp}
\begin{aligned}
\left\|J_1-\widetilde J_1\right\|_p^2
\le&\,
C\int_t^{t+\varepsilon}\int_{\mathbb R^2}
|D_{t+\varepsilon-s}(x-y,h)|^2
\left\|\xi_1(s,y)\right\|_p^2
|h|^{2H-2}\mathrm d y\mathrm d h\mathrm d s\\
&+C\int_t^{t+\varepsilon}\int_\mathbb R
G_{t+\varepsilon-s}(x-y)^2
\bigl[\mathcal N_{1/2-H,p}\sigma(u(s,\cdot))(y)\bigr]^2
\mathrm d y\mathrm d s.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Substituting the preceding coefficient bounds into
\eqref{eq:J1-error-decomp} and applying
\eqref{t:eq:kernel-L2}-\eqref{t:eq:kernel-weighted}
with $r=t+\varepsilon-s$, we obtain
$$
\begin{aligned}
\left\|J_1-\widetilde J_1\right\|_p^2
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}\int_0^\varepsilon
\bigl(
(\varepsilon-r)^{2\vartheta}r^{H-1}
+r^{H+2\vartheta-1}
+r^{-1/2}
\bigr)\mathrm d r\\
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}
\bigl(\varepsilon^{H+2\vartheta}+\varepsilon^{1/2}\bigr)\\
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}\varepsilon^{H+2\vartheta},
\end{aligned}
$$
where the last inequality uses $\varepsilon<1$ and
$H+2\vartheta<1/2$.
Taking square roots proves \eqref{t:eq:J1-bound}.

 \noindent\emph{Step 2.}
Split $J_{2,\beta}=I_1+I_2$, where $I_1$ and $I_2$ are the
integrals over $[0,T_0/2]$ and $[T_0/2,t-\varepsilon^\beta]$, respectively.

For $I_1$, the semigroup property and
Lemma~\ref{lem:semigroup-fubini} give
\begin{equation*}                   
\begin{aligned}
I_1
= \,
\int_\mathbb R
\bigl[G_{t+\varepsilon-T_0/2}(z)-G_{t-T_0/2}(z)\bigr] 
\bigl[u(T_0/2,x-z)-(G_{T_0/2}*u_0)(x-z)\bigr]\mathrm d z.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
The Gaussian decay of the heat-kernel derivatives implies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:heat-kernel-time-weights}
\sup_{\rho\in[T_0/2,T+1]}
\int_\mathbb R
|\partial_\rho G_\rho(z)|
(1+|z|)^{2(1-H)/q}\mathrm d z
<\infty.
\end{equation}
By Minkowski's inequality, \eqref{eq:umom}, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:initial-smoothing}(i)--(ii),
$$
\begin{aligned}
\left\|I_1\right\|_p
\le&\,
\int_\mathbb R
\bigl|G_{t+\varepsilon-T_0/2}(z)-G_{t-T_0/2}(z)\bigr| 
\bigl\|u(T_0/2,x-z)
-(G_{T_0/2}*u_0)(x-z)\bigr\|_p\mathrm d z\\
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-1/q}
\int_\mathbb R
\bigl|G_{t+\varepsilon-T_0/2}(z)-G_{t-T_0/2}(z)\bigr|
(1+|z|)^{2(1-H)/q}\mathrm d z\\
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-1/q}\varepsilon.
\end{aligned}
$$
Here the last inequality follows from the fundamental theorem
of calculus and \eqref{eq:heat-kernel-time-weights}.                                                                       

For $I_2$, applying \eqref{eq:BDG-product} and using
the Lipschitz continuity of $\sigma$, \eqref{eq:umom},
and \eqref{eq:N-seminorm-sigma}, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:I2-bound}
\begin{aligned}
\left\|I_2\right\|_p^2
\le&\,
C\int_{T_0/2}^{t-\varepsilon^\beta}\int_{\mathbb R^2}
|D_{t+\varepsilon-s}(x-y,h)-D_{t-s}(x-y,h)|^2
\lambda(y)^{-2/q}|h|^{2H-2}\mathrm d y\mathrm d h\mathrm d s\\
&+C\int_{T_0/2}^{t-\varepsilon^\beta}\int_\mathbb R
|G_{t+\varepsilon-s}(x-y)-G_{t-s}(x-y)|^2
\lambda(y)^{-2/q}\mathrm d y\mathrm d s\\
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}
\bigl(\varepsilon^{2+\beta(H-2)}+\varepsilon^{1/2}\bigr),
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where the last inequality follows from
Lemma~\ref{t:lem:integrated}(i)-(ii), applied with
$r=t-s\ge\varepsilon^\beta$.
Taking square roots in \eqref{eq:I2-bound} and combining
the estimates for $I_1$ and $I_2$ by the triangle inequality
proves \eqref{t:eq:J2-bound}.                                                 

\noindent
\emph{Step 3. }
Set $\tau:=t-\varepsilon^\beta$. 
                                                                                                                            
Define
$$
Z_{t,\varepsilon}
:=\int_\tau^t\int_\mathbb R
\bigl[G_{t+\varepsilon-s}(x-y)-G_{t-s}(x-y)\bigr]
W(\mathrm d s,\mathrm d y)
$$
and write
$$
J_{3,\beta}-\widetilde J_{3,\beta}=K_1+K_2,
$$
where
$$
\begin{aligned}
K_1:=&\,
J_{3,\beta}-\sigma(u(\tau,x))Z_{t,\varepsilon},\\
K_2:=&\,
\bigl[\sigma(u(\tau,x))-\sigma(u(t,x))\bigr]Z_{t,\varepsilon}.
\end{aligned}
$$

For $K_1$, set
$$
\xi_3(s,y):=\sigma(u(s,y))-\sigma(u(\tau,x)),
\qquad \tau<s\le t.
$$
As in Step 1, $\xi_3$ is predictable on $(\tau,t]$ and has
the same spatial fractional seminorm as $\sigma(u(s,\cdot))$.
The coefficient increment estimate from that step, together
with $s-\tau\le\varepsilon^\beta$, also gives
\begin{equation}\label{Eq:xi3}
\left\|\xi_3(s,y)\right\|_p^2
\le
C\bigl(\lambda(y)^{-2/q}+\lambda(x)^{-2/q}\bigr)
\bigl(\varepsilon^{2\beta\vartheta}+|x-y|^{4\vartheta}\bigr).
\end{equation}
Applying \eqref{eq:BDG-product} to $K_1$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:I1-error-decomp}
\begin{aligned}
\left\|K_1\right\|_p^2
\le&\,
C\int_\tau^t\int_{\mathbb R^2}
|D_{t+\varepsilon-s}(x-y,h)-D_{t-s}(x-y,h)|^2
\left\|\xi_3(s,y)\right\|_p^2
|h|^{2H-2}\mathrm d y\mathrm d h\mathrm d s\\
&+C\int_\tau^t\int_\mathbb R
|G_{t+\varepsilon-s}(x-y)-G_{t-s}(x-y)|^2
\bigl[\mathcal N_{1/2-H,p}\sigma(u(s,\cdot))(y)\bigr]^2
\mathrm d y\mathrm d s.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
For the kernel difference in the first integral, we use
$$
\begin{aligned}
 |D_{t+\varepsilon-s}(x-y,h)-D_{t-s}(x-y,h)|^2 
\le \,
2|D_{t-s}(x-y,h)|^2
+2|D_{t+\varepsilon-s}(x-y,h)|^2.
\end{aligned}
$$
Using this inequality,  
  \eqref{eq:N-seminorm-sigma}, and \eqref{Eq:xi3}, we apply
Lemma~\ref{t:lem:integrated}(ii)-(iii) to the two integrals in
\eqref{eq:I1-error-decomp}, with $r=t-s\in[0,\varepsilon^\beta]$, to obtain
$$
 \left\|K_1\right\|_p^2
 \le C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}
 \bigl(\varepsilon^{\beta(H+2\vartheta)}+\varepsilon^{1/2}\bigr).
$$
Since $\varepsilon<1$ and $\beta(H+2\vartheta)<1/2$,
taking square roots yields
$$
\left\|K_1\right\|_p
\le C\lambda(x)^{-1/q}
\varepsilon^{\beta(H/2+\vartheta)}.
$$

To estimate $K_2$, we use the Gaussianity of $Z_{t,\varepsilon}$ and Lemma~\ref{t:lem:integrated}(iii)
to obtain
$$
 \left\|Z_{t,\varepsilon}\right\|_{2p}
 \le C\left\|Z_{t,\varepsilon}\right\|_2
 \le C\varepsilon^{\beta H/2}.
$$
 By H\"older's inequality and the Lipschitz continuity of $\sigma$, we have 
$$
\begin{aligned}
\left\|K_2\right\|_p
\le&\,
\left\|\sigma(u(\tau,x))-\sigma(u(t,x))\right\|_{2p}
\left\|Z_{t,\varepsilon}\right\|_{2p}\\
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-1/q}\varepsilon^{\beta H}.
\end{aligned}
$$ 

Combining the estimates for $K_1$ and $K_2$ by the triangle
inequality proves \eqref{t:eq:refreeze-bound}. 
The proof is complete.

title: Proof
body_md:
We follow the localization strategy used in
\cite[Proposition~4.6]{KSXZ2014},
\cite[Theorem~1.2]{Qian2026}, and
\cite[Theorem~1.2]{WangXiao2024}.

Fix $0<T_0<T<\infty$, $q_H<q\le q_0$, and $0<\delta<\delta_t(q)$. 
Define
$$
\delta(\vartheta):=\frac{(2-H)\vartheta}{2(1+\vartheta)}.
$$
Since $\delta(\vartheta)$ is continuous and strictly increasing,
with $\delta(\vartheta_q)=\delta_t(q)$, we may choose
$0<\vartheta<\vartheta_q$ such that $\delta<\delta(\vartheta)$.
To balance the error exponents, set
$\beta:=1/(1+\vartheta)\in(0,1)$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{t:eq:balance}
2+\beta(H-2)
=\beta(H+2\vartheta)
=H+2\delta(\vartheta).
\end{equation}
Choose $\varepsilon_0\in(0,1)$ sufficiently small that
$\varepsilon_0^\beta<T_0/4$.

Let $2\le p\le q/2$ and $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$.
For  $t\in[T_0,T]$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, by \eqref{eq:Jdecomp}-\eqref{eq:J3approx}, we have 
\begin{equation}\label{Eq:Rt}
\begin{aligned}
R^{\mathrm t}(t,x,\varepsilon)
=&\,
(G_{t+\varepsilon}*u_0)(x)-(G_t*u_0)(x) +(J_1-\widetilde J_1)+J_{2,\beta}
 +(J_{3,\beta}-\widetilde J_{3,\beta})\\
&-\sigma(u(t,x))
\int_0^{t-\varepsilon^\beta}\int_\mathbb R
\bigl[G_{t+\varepsilon-s}(x-y)-G_{t-s}(x-y)\bigr]
W(\mathrm d s,\mathrm d y).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}




For the initial term in \eqref{Eq:Rt}, the fundamental theorem
of calculus, Minkowski's inequality, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:initial-smoothing}(ii) yield
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\sup_{T_0\le t\le T}\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}
\lambda(x)^{1/q}
\left\|(G_{t+\varepsilon}*u_0)(x)-(G_t*u_0)(x)\right\|_p\\
\le&\,
\varepsilon\sup_{T_0\le s\le T+1}\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}
\lambda(x)^{1/q}
\left\|\partial_x^2(G_s*u_0)(x)\right\|_p\\
\le&\,C\varepsilon,
\end{aligned}
$$
where we used
$\partial_s(G_s*u_0)=\partial_x^2(G_s*u_0)$.
 

For the last term in (\ref{Eq:Rt}), H\"older's inequality,
\eqref{eq:umom}, Gaussian moment comparison, and the unweighted
version of Lemma~\ref{t:lem:integrated}(i) give
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\left\|
\sigma(u(t,x))
\int_0^{t-\varepsilon^\beta}\int_\mathbb R
\bigl[G_{t+\varepsilon-s}(x-y)-G_{t-s}(x-y)\bigr]
W(\mathrm d s,\mathrm d y)
\right\|_p\\
\le&\,
\left\|\sigma(u(t,x))\right\|_{2p}
\left\|
\int_0^{t-\varepsilon^\beta}\int_\mathbb R
\bigl[G_{t+\varepsilon-s}(x-y)-G_{t-s}(x-y)\bigr]
W(\mathrm d s,\mathrm d y)
\right\|_{2p}\\
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-1/q}\varepsilon^{1+\beta(H/2-1)}.
\end{aligned}
$$ 

Combining these bounds with Lemma~\ref{t:lem:errors}
and using \eqref{t:eq:balance}, we obtain
$$
\begin{aligned}
 \sup_{T_0\le t\le T}\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}
\lambda(x)^{1/q}\left\|R^{\mathrm t}(t,x,\varepsilon)\right\|_p 
\le&\,
C\bigl(
\varepsilon
+\varepsilon^{H/2+\vartheta}
+\varepsilon^{H/2+\delta(\vartheta)}
+\varepsilon^{1/4}
\bigr)\\
\le&\,
C\varepsilon^{H/2+\delta},
\end{aligned}
$$
where the last inequality uses $0<\varepsilon<1$ and
$\delta<\delta(\vartheta)<\vartheta<1/4-H/2$.

This proves \eqref{t:eq:main-moment} for
$2\le p\le q/2$ and $\varepsilon > 0$.
After decreasing $\varepsilon_0$ if necessary,                     
the remainder $R^{\mathrm t}(t,x,\varepsilon)$ can be 
 handled similarly for $\varepsilon < 0$,                                                                                                                                       
 using $t+\varepsilon$ as the base point.
For $1\le p<2$, the same estimate follows from the 
  monotonicity of $L^p$ norms. The proof is complete.

label: eq:As
title: Proof
body_md:
\noindent
\emph{(i)}
For $t-\rho\le s\le t$, set
$$
A_s(y):=\sigma(u(s,y))-\sigma(u(t-\rho,x)).
$$
Since $\sigma(u(t-\rho,x))$ is
$\mathcal F_{t-\rho}$-measurable, $A$ is predictable on
$(t-\rho,t]$, and
$$
J_{\mathrm n}-\widetilde J_{\mathrm n}
=
\int_{t-\rho}^t\int_\mathbb R
D_{t-s}(x-y,\varepsilon)A_s(y)\,W(\mathrm d s,\mathrm d y).
$$
Since $\rho<1$, the Lipschitz continuity
of $\sigma$ and \eqref{eq:exact-holder}, together with
\eqref{eq:umom} for $|y-x|>1$, give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:As}
\left\|A_s(y)\right\|_{p}^2
\le
C\bigl[\lambda(y)^{-2/q}+\lambda(x)^{-2/q}\bigr]
\bigl[\rho^H+(|y-x|^{2H}\wedge1)\bigr].
\end{equation}
Moreover, the frozen value does not depend on $y$, so
the Lipschitz continuity of $\sigma$ and \eqref{eq:ufrac} imply
\begin{align}\label{eq NA}
\mathcal N_{1/2-H,p}A_s(y)
=
\mathcal N_{1/2-H,p}\sigma(u(s,\cdot))(y)
\le C\lambda(y)^{-1/q}.
\end{align} 
 

Applying \eqref{eq:BDG-product}, we obtain
$$
\left\|J_{\mathrm n}-\widetilde J_{\mathrm n}\right\|_p^2
\le C(B_1+B_2),
$$
where
$$
\begin{aligned}
B_1:=&\,
\int_{t-\rho}^t\int_{\mathbb R^2}
|D_{t-s}(x-y-h,\varepsilon)-D_{t-s}(x-y,\varepsilon)|^2
\left\|A_s(y+h)\right\|_{p}^2
|h|^{2H-2}\mathrm d h\mathrm d y\mathrm d s,\\
B_2:=&\,
\int_{t-\rho}^t\int_\mathbb R
|D_{t-s}(x-y,\varepsilon)|^2
\bigl[
\mathcal N_{1/2-H,p}\sigma(u(s,\cdot))(y)
\bigr]^2
\mathrm d y\mathrm d s.
\end{aligned}
$$

For $B_1$, set $r=t-s$ and $z=x-y-h$, so that
$A_s(y+h)=A_{t-r}(x-z)$.
By \eqref{eq:As}, Lemma~\ref{lem:initial-smoothing}(i),
and Lemma~\ref{lem:weightedenergy},
$$
\begin{aligned}
B_1
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}\int_0^\rho\int_{\mathbb R^2}
|D_r(z+h,\varepsilon)-D_r(z,\varepsilon)|^2(1+|z|)^{a_q} 
\bigl[\rho^H+(|z|^{2H}\wedge1)\bigr]
|h|^{2H-2}\mathrm d h\mathrm d z\mathrm d r\\
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}
\bigl(\rho^H\varepsilon^{2H}+\varepsilon^{4H}+\varepsilon\bigr).
\end{aligned}
$$
For $B_2$, use $r=t-s$ and $z=x-y$. By \eqref{eq NA},  
Lemmas~\ref{lem:initial-smoothing}(i) and
\ref{lem:singleenergy}(i), we have 
$$
\begin{aligned}
B_2
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}
\int_0^\rho\int_\mathbb R
|D_r(z,\varepsilon)|^2(1+|z|)^{a_q}\mathrm d z\mathrm d r\\
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}\varepsilon.
\end{aligned}
$$
Combining the bounds for $B_1$ and $B_2$ and taking
square roots proves \eqref{eq:freeze}.

\noindent
\emph{(ii)}
The Gaussianity of $L_{\mathrm n}$,  \eqref{eq:stochastic-isometry},
and Lemma~\ref{lem:energy} give 
$$
\left\|L_{\mathrm n}\right\|_{2p}
\le C\left\|L_{\mathrm n}\right\|_{2}
\le C\varepsilon^H.
$$
 By H\"older's inequality, the Lipschitz continuity of $\sigma$, and \eqref{eq:exact-holder}, we have 
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\lambda(x)^{1/q}
\left\|[\sigma(u(t-\rho,x))-\sigma(u(t,x))]L_{\mathrm n}\right\|_{p}\\
\le&\,
\lambda(x)^{1/q}
\left\|\sigma(u(t-\rho,x))-\sigma(u(t,x))\right\|_{2p} \cdot
\left\|L_{\mathrm n}\right\|_{2p}\\
\le&\,
C\varepsilon^H\rho^{H/2}.
\end{aligned}
$$ 
This proves \eqref{eq:freeze-coeff}.

Let $q_H<q\le q_0$, $2\le p\le q/2$,
$0<\rho<1\wedge(T_0/2)$, and
$0<\varepsilon\le\sqrt{\rho}$.
Then

\left(
\left\|J_{\mathrm f}\right\|_{p} +

label: eq:remoteconv
title: Proof
body_md:
By the heat-semigroup property and
Lemma~\ref{lem:semigroup-fubini},
\[
J_{\mathrm f}
=
\int_\mathbb R D_\rho(z,\varepsilon)
\bigl[u(t-\rho,x-z)-(G_{t-\rho}*u_0)(x-z)\bigr]\mathrm d z.
\]
Since $\int_\mathbb R D_\rho(z,\varepsilon)\mathrm d z=0$, we may write
\begin{equation}\label{eq:remoteconv}
\begin{aligned}
J_{\mathrm f}
=\int_\mathbb R D_\rho(z,\varepsilon)\bigl\{
&u(t-\rho,x-z)-u(t-\rho,x)\\
&-(G_{t-\rho}*u_0)(x-z)+(G_{t-\rho}*u_0)(x)
\bigr\}\mathrm d z.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

By \eqref{eq:umom} and \eqref{eq:exact-holder}, we have 
\[
\left\|u(t-\rho,x-z)-u(t-\rho,x)\right\|_{p}
\le
C\bigl[\lambda(x-z)^{-1/q}+\lambda(x)^{-1/q}\bigr]
\left(|z|^H\wedge1\right).
\]

Similarly, using \eqref{eq:msmooth} with $j=0,1$, we obtain
$$
\left\|
(G_{t-\rho}*u_0)(x-z)-(G_{t-\rho}*u_0)(x)
\right\|_p
\le
C\bigl[\lambda(x-z)^{-1/q}+\lambda(x)^{-1/q}\bigr]
(|z|\wedge1).
$$
It follows from \eqref{eq:remoteconv}, Minkowski's inequality,   and
Lemmas~\ref{lem:initial-smoothing}(i) and~\ref{lem:singleenergy}(ii) that
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left\|J_{\mathrm f}\right\|_{p}
\le &\,
C\lambda(x)^{-1/q}
\int_\mathbb R |D_\rho(z,\varepsilon)|
(1+|z|)^{2(1-H)/q}
\left(|z|^H\wedge1\right)\mathrm d z\\
\le &\,
C\lambda(x)^{-1/q}\varepsilon\rho^{-(1-H)/2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

By  H\"older's inequality and \eqref{eq:umom}, we have
\[
\lambda(x)^{1/q}
\left\|\sigma(u(t,x))L_{\mathrm f}\right\|_{p}
\le
C\left\|L_{\mathrm f}\right\|_{2p}.
\]
By \eqref{eq:stochastic-isometry}, we have 
 \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E|L_{\mathrm f}|^2
&\le
C\int_\rho^\infty\int_\mathbb R
e^{-2r\xi^2}|e^{i\varepsilon\xi}-1|^2
|\xi|^{1-2H}\mathrm d\xi\mathrm d r\\
&\le
C\varepsilon^2\int_\rho^\infty\int_\mathbb R
e^{-2r\xi^2}|\xi|^{3-2H}\mathrm d\xi\mathrm d r\\
&=
C\varepsilon^2\int_\rho^\infty
r^{H-2}
\left(
\int_\mathbb R e^{-2z^2}|z|^{3-2H}\mathrm d z
\right)\mathrm d r\\
&\le
C\varepsilon^2\rho^{H-1},
\end{aligned}
\]
where in the third line we used the change of variables
$z=\sqrt r\,\xi$.
Gaussian moment equivalence therefore gives
\[
\lambda(x)^{1/q}
\left\|\sigma(u(t,x))L_{\mathrm f}\right\|_{p}
\le
C\varepsilon\rho^{-(1-H)/2}.
\]
This proves the lemma.

label: eq:Rx-decomp
title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $0<T_0<T<\infty$, $q_H<q\le q_0$, and
$0<\delta<\delta_x^*$. We first estimate
$R^{\mathrm x}(t,x,\varepsilon)$ for $2\le p\le q/2$ and
$0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$. Set $\rho:=\varepsilon^{2(1-H)}$ and choose
$\varepsilon_0\in(0,1)$ sufficiently small that
$$
 0<\rho<1\wedge(T_0/2),
 \qquad
 \varepsilon\le\sqrt{\rho}.
$$ 

For $t\in[T_0,T]$ and $x\in\mathbb R$,
\eqref{eq:spatial-u-decomp}--\eqref{eq:Jn-approx} give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Rx-decomp}
\begin{aligned}
R^{\mathrm x}(t,x,\varepsilon)
=&\,
(G_t*u_0)(x+\varepsilon)-(G_t*u_0)(x)\\
&+\bigl[J_{\mathrm f}-\sigma(u(t,x))L_{\mathrm f}\bigr]
+\bigl[J_{\mathrm n}-\widetilde J_{\mathrm n}\bigr]\\
&+\bigl[\sigma(u(t-\rho,x))-\sigma(u(t,x))\bigr]
L_{\mathrm n}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The fundamental theorem of calculus, Minkowski's inequality,
and Lemma~\ref{lem:initial-smoothing}(i)--(ii) yield
$$
\lambda(x)^{1/q}
\left\|(G_t*u_0)(x+\varepsilon)-(G_t*u_0)(x)\right\|_p
\le C\varepsilon.
$$
Using Lemmas~\ref{lem:freeze} and \ref{lem:remote} in
\eqref{eq:Rx-decomp}, we obtain
$$
\begin{aligned}
\lambda(x)^{1/q}\left\|R^{\mathrm x}(t,x,\varepsilon)\right\|_{p}
\le&\,
C\Bigl(
\varepsilon
+\varepsilon\rho^{-(1-H)/2}
+\varepsilon^H\rho^{H/2}
+\varepsilon^{2H}
+\varepsilon^{1/2}
\Bigr)\\
\le&\,
C\Bigl(
\varepsilon
+\varepsilon^{H+H(1-H)}
+\varepsilon^{2H}
+\varepsilon^{1/2}
\Bigr),
\end{aligned}
$$
uniformly for $t\in[T_0,T]$ and $x\in\mathbb R$.
Since $H>1/4$, we have 
$\varepsilon^{2H}\le\varepsilon^{1/2}$ for $0<\varepsilon<1$.
Moreover,
$$
\delta<\delta_x^*
=
\min\left\{H(1-H),\frac12-H\right\}.
$$
Therefore,
$$
\sup_{T_0\le t\le T}\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}
\lambda(x)^{1/q}\left\|R^{\mathrm x}(t,x,\varepsilon)\right\|_{p}
\le C\varepsilon^{H+\delta},
\qquad 0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0.
$$


The remainder $R^{\mathrm x}(t,x,\varepsilon)$ for $\varepsilon<0$ is handled similarly by
shifting the base point to $x+\varepsilon$.
For $1\le p<2$, the same estimate follows from 
 the monotonicity of $L^p$ norms. The proof is complete.

label: lemma:pathwise
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove only part (ii) in detail.  
Part (i) follows by the same grid interpolation argument, using the temporal moment and H\"older estimates. It gives a version of \cite[Lemma~5.1]{Qian2026} that holds uniformly over compact time intervals.



Fix $t>0$, compact intervals $J,\widetilde J\subset\mathbb R$ with
$J\subset\operatorname{int}(\widetilde J)$, and
$0<\delta_x<\delta_{x,\mathrm{pw}}$. Set $P:=q_0/2$.
By \eqref{eq:delta-x-pw}, we can choose $m>1$ such that
$$
 \frac{H+\delta_x}{H-1/q_0}
 <m<
 \frac{P(\delta_x^*-\delta_x)+1}{2}.
$$
The strict inequalities allow us to choose
$\delta_x<\delta_1<\delta_2<\delta_x^*$ and
$0<\zeta<H-1/q_0$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pathwise-parameter-choice}
 m\zeta>H+\delta_x,
 \qquad
 P(\delta_2-\delta_1)+1-2m>0.
\end{equation} 

Since $\lambda$ is bounded away from zero on $\widetilde J$,
Theorem~\ref{thm:local-linearization}(ii), applied with $q=q_0$
and $p=P$, yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pathwise-space-moment}
 \|R^{\mathrm x}(t,x,y-x)\|_{P}
 \le C|y-x|^{H+\delta_2}
\end{equation}
for all $x,y\in\widetilde J$ with $|y-x|$ sufficiently small.

  Combining   \eqref{eq:U-increment-Lp} and \eqref{eq:exact-holder} with $p=q=q_0$, and using the compactness of $\widetilde J$, we obtain 
\[
 \mathbb E|u(t,x)-u(t,y)|^{q_0}
 +\mathbb E|U(t,x)-U(t,y)|^{q_0}
 \le C|x-y|^{q_0H},
 \qquad x,y\in \widetilde J.
\]

Since $q_0H>1$, Kolmogorov's continuity theorem
(see, e.g., \cite[p.~10]{DKMNX}) yields continuous versions of
$u(t,\cdot)$ and $U(t,\cdot)$,  whose sample paths are almost surely
$\zeta$-H\"older continuous on $\widetilde J$ for the chosen
$\zeta\in(0,H-1/q_0)$.  Their H\"older continuity and boundedness on $\widetilde J$,
together with the Lipschitz continuity of $\sigma$, imply
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pathwise-space-interpolation}
\begin{aligned}
  |R^{\mathrm x}(t,x,y-x)-R^{\mathrm x}(t,\bar x,\bar y-\bar x)| \le C(\omega)\bigl(|x-\bar x|^\zeta+|y-\bar y|^\zeta\bigr),
 \quad x,y,\bar x,\bar y\in \widetilde J,
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where $C(\omega)<\infty$ almost surely.

 Let $r_n=2^{-n}$, $a_n=r_n^m$, and
$$
 \mathcal G_n=(a_n\mathbb Z)^2\cap(\widetilde J\times\widetilde J).
$$
The interval $\widetilde J$ contains $O(a_n^{-1})$ grid points $x$. For each such $x$, the interval $[x-2r_n,x+2r_n]$ contains
$O(r_n/a_n)$ grid points $y$.  Hence,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pathwise-grid-count}
 \#\{\,(x,y)\in\mathcal G_n:|y-x|\le2r_n\,\}
 \le Cr_na_n^{-2}=Cr_n^{1-2m}.
\end{equation}



 For all sufficiently large $n$,  by Markov's
inequality,   \eqref{eq:pathwise-space-moment},
and \eqref{eq:pathwise-grid-count},  we have 
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb P\left\{
 \max_{\substack{(x,y)\in\mathcal G_n\\|y-x|\le2r_n}}
 |R^{\mathrm x}(t,x,y-x)|>r_n^{H+\delta_1}
 \right\} 
 \le &\,
 r_n^{-P(H+\delta_1)}
 \sum_{\substack{(x,y)\in\mathcal G_n\\|y-x|\le2r_n}}
 \|R^{\mathrm x}(t,x,y-x)\|_{P}^P\\
 \le &\,  Cr_n^{P(\delta_2-\delta_1)+1-2m}.
\end{align*}
By \eqref{eq:pathwise-parameter-choice}, the exponent in the last term 
is positive, so these probabilities are summable. The Borel--Cantelli 
lemma therefore yields, almost surely, for all sufficiently large $n$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pathwise-grid-bound}
 \max_{\substack{(x,y)\in\mathcal G_n\\|y-x|\le2r_n}}
 |R^{\mathrm x}(t,x,y-x)|\le r_n^{H+\delta_1}.
\end{equation} 

Since $J\subset\operatorname{int}(\widetilde J)$ and $a_n=o(r_n)$,
for all sufficiently large $n$ and all $x,y\in J$ with
$|y-x|\le r_n$, we can choose $(\bar x,\bar y)\in\mathcal G_n$
such that
$$
 |x-\bar x|+|y-\bar y|\le2a_n,
 \qquad
 |\bar y-\bar x|\le r_n+2a_n\le2r_n.
$$
 
Combining \eqref{eq:pathwise-space-interpolation} and
\eqref{eq:pathwise-grid-bound} yields, almost surely,
\[
 \sup_{\substack{x,y\in J\\|y-x|\le r_n}}
 |R^{\mathrm x}(t,x,y-x)|
 \le C(\omega)r_n^{m\zeta}+r_n^{H+\delta_1}
 =o(r_n^{H+\delta_x}).
\]
Since the supremum is nondecreasing in $r$ and $r_n/r_{n+1}=2$,
the estimate extends to arbitrary $r\downarrow0$, proving
\eqref{eq:spatial-pathwise} for the  chosen $J$ and $\delta_x$. 


Taking the intersection over all $k\ge1$ and
$\gamma\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,\delta_{x,\mathrm{pw}})$,
we obtain a single event of probability one on which
\eqref{eq:spatial-pathwise} holds with $J=J_k:=[-k,k]$
and $\delta_x=\gamma$ for every such pair $(k,\gamma)$.
Now fix any compact interval $J\subset\mathbb R$ and
$0<\delta_x<\delta_{x,\mathrm{pw}}$.
Choose $k\ge1$ such that $J\subset J_k$ and
a rational number $\gamma$ satisfying
$\delta_x<\gamma<\delta_{x,\mathrm{pw}}$.
On the same probability-one event, the estimate on $J_k$
with exponent $\gamma$ also holds on $J$.
Since
\[
r^{H+\gamma}=o(r^{H+\delta_x})
\qquad\text{as }r\downarrow0,
\]
the desired assertion follows simultaneously for all
such $J$ and $\delta_x$.
 
  
 The proof is complete.

label: lem:completion

label: lem:fbm-laws
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $(t,x)\in(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$. We follow the argument
in~\cite{FKM2015,WangXiao2024}.
Let $\alpha=H$ for spatial increments and $\alpha=H/2$ for
temporal increments. By Lemmas~\ref{lemma:pathwise} and
\ref{lem:completion}, the remainders and smooth correction terms
are negligible relative to
$$
 r^\alpha\sqrt{2\log\log(1/r)},
 \qquad
 \left(\frac{r}{\log\log(1/r)}\right)^\alpha,
$$
the normalizing factors in Lemma~\ref{lem:fbm-laws}(i)--(ii),
respectively.   The assertions then follow.

label: rem:normalized-moduli
title: Remark
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For the spatial assertion \eqref{eq:spatial-modulus}, assume
$\delta_{x,\mathrm{pw}}>0$ and fix $t>0$.
Let
\[
\mathcal Q=\{[a,b]:a,b\in\mathbb Q,\ a<b\}.
\]

 

\noindent\emph{Step 1: A common probability-one event.}
Let $B_t^H$ and $S_t$ be the processes in
Lemma~\ref{lem:completion}(i). By Lemma~\ref{lem:fbm-laws}(iii)
and the countability of $\mathcal Q$, there is a probability-one
event on which
\begin{align}\label{eq LILsim}
\lim_{r\downarrow0}
\sup_{\substack{x,y\in I\\ |y-x|\le r}}
\frac{|B_t^H(y)-B_t^H(x)|}{r^H\sqrt{2\log(1/r)}}
=1
\qquad\text{for every }I\in\mathcal Q.
\end{align}

 Work on a common probability-one event $\Omega_t^{\mathrm{sp}}$
on which \eqref{eq LILsim} and the conclusion of  Lemma~\ref{lemma:pathwise}(ii) hold,
$S_t$ is smooth, and $\sigma(u(t,\cdot))$ is continuous.
For an arbitrary nondegenerate compact interval
$J=[a,b]\subset\mathbb R$, set
\[
M_J:=\max_{x\in J}|\sigma(u(t,x))|.
\]

 
   \noindent\emph{Step 2: Upper bound.} Fix $0<\delta_x<\delta_{x,\mathrm{pw}}$.
By \eqref{eq Rx} and Lemma~\ref{lem:completion}(i),
for $x,y\in J$ with $|y-x|\le r$, we have 
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\left|
u(t,y)-u(t,x)
-\frac{\sigma(u(t,x))}{\sqrt2}
\bigl(B_t^H(y)-B_t^H(x)\bigr)
\right|\\
 \le&\, 
|R^{\mathrm x}(t,x,y-x)|
+
|\sigma(u(t,x))|\,|S_t(y)-S_t(x)|\\
 \le &\, 
 |R^{\mathrm x}(t,x,y-x)|
+
M_J\sup_{z\in J}|S_t'(z)|\,r.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here we used the smoothness of $S_t$ on $\mathbb R$ and the fact that
$J$ is compact. Define
\[
d_J(r)
:=
\sup_{\substack{x,y\in J\\ |y-x|\le r}}
|R^{\mathrm x}(t,x,y-x)|
+
M_J\sup_{z\in J}|S_t'(z)|\,r.
\]

Since $H<1$ and $\delta_x>0$, \eqref{eq:spatial-pathwise} gives 
\begin{align}\label{eq dj}
\lim_{r\downarrow 0}\frac{d_J(r)}{r^H\sqrt{2\log(1/r)}}
=0, \ \ \text{ a.s.}
\end{align}

Let
\[
\omega_{t,J}(r)
:=
\sup_{\substack{x,y\in J\\ |y-x|\le r}}
|u(t,y)-u(t,x)|.
\]
Taking the supremum in the above estimate gives
\[
\omega_{t,J}(r)
\le
\frac{M_J}{\sqrt2}
\sup_{\substack{x,y\in J\\ |y-x|\le r}}
|B_t^H(y)-B_t^H(x)|
+d_J(r).
\] 
Choose $K\in\mathcal Q$ containing $J$. By \eqref{eq LILsim} and \eqref{eq dj}, we have
\[
\limsup_{r\downarrow0}
\frac{\omega_{t,J}(r)}{r^H\sqrt{2\log(1/r)}}
\le \frac{M_J}{\sqrt2}.
\]
 
 
\noindent\emph{Step 3: Lower bound.}
If $M_J=0$, the conclusion follows immediately from the upper bound.
Assume now that $M_J>0$ and fix $0<\eta<M_J$.

By the continuity of $\sigma(u(t,\cdot))$, the set
\[
\{x\in(a,b): |\sigma(u(t,x))|>M_J-\eta\}
\]
is a nonempty open subset of $(a,b)$. Hence, it contains a
nondegenerate compact interval
$I_\eta\subset J$ with rational endpoints such that
\[
|\sigma(u(t,x))|\ge M_J-\eta,
\qquad x\in I_\eta.
\]
Thus $I_\eta\in\mathcal Q$.

For $x,y\in I_\eta$ with $|y-x|\le r$, the estimate from
Step~2 gives
\[
|u(t,y)-u(t,x)|
\ge
\frac{M_J-\eta}{\sqrt2}
|B_t^H(y)-B_t^H(x)|
-d_J(r).
\]
By \eqref{eq LILsim} and \eqref{eq dj},
\[
\liminf_{r\downarrow0}
\frac{\omega_{t,J}(r)}{r^H\sqrt{2\log(1/r)}}
\ge
\frac{M_J-\eta}{\sqrt2}.
\]
Letting $\eta\downarrow0$ and combining this lower bound with
the upper bound proves \eqref{eq:spatial-modulus} simultaneously for
every nondegenerate compact interval $J$ on $\Omega_t^{\mathrm{sp}}$.

For the temporal assertion, fix $x\in\mathbb R$ and assume
$\delta_{t,\mathrm{pw}}>0$.  The same argument applies with
Lemmas \ref{lemma:pathwise}(i), \ref{lem:completion}(ii), and \ref{lem:fbm-laws}(iii),   replacing $H$ and
$1/\sqrt{2}$ by $H/2$ and $\gamma_H$, respectively.
Using compact intervals with rational endpoints in $(0,\infty)$
to construct the common probability-one event yields
\eqref{eq:temporal-modulus} simultaneously for every nondegenerate
compact interval $I\subset(0,\infty)$.

The proof is complete.

label: lem:schwartz
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $|z|\le2$, we apply the mean-value theorem when $|h|\le1$
and use the boundedness of $f$ when $|h|>1$ to obtain 
$$
\begin{aligned}
Q_Hf(z)
\le&\,
\left\|f'\right\|_\infty^2
\int_{|h|\le1}|h|^{2H}\mathrm d h
+
4\left\|f\right\|_\infty^2
\int_{|h|>1}|h|^{2H-2}\mathrm d h\\
\le&\, C_{f,H}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Now let $|z|>2$ and split the integral at $|h|=|z|/2$.
For $|h|\le|z|/2$, the rapid decay of $f$ and $f'$ yields
$$
|f(z+h)-f(z)|
\le
C_f(1+|z|)^{-1}(|h|\wedge1),
$$
and hence
$$
\int_{|h|\le|z|/2}
|f(z+h)-f(z)|^2|h|^{2H-2}\mathrm d h
\le
C_{f,H}(1+|z|)^{-2}.
$$
On the complementary region, using
$|a-b|^2\le2|a|^2+2|b|^2$, we obtain 
$$
\begin{aligned}
 \int_{|h|>|z|/2}
|f(z+h)-f(z)|^2|h|^{2H-2}\mathrm d h 
\le&\,
C_H|z|^{2H-2}\left\|f\right\|_{L^2(\mathbb R)}^2
+
C_H|f(z)|^2|z|^{2H-1}\\
\le&\,
C_{f,H}(1+|z|)^{2H-2}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Since
$$
(1+|z|)^{-2}\le(1+|z|)^{2H-2},
$$
the desired estimate follows.

label: t:lem:kernels
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{t:lem:kernels}
Let $q_H<q\le q_0$, $0<r\le T$, $0<\varepsilon<1$, and
$$
0\le\vartheta<\frac{1-2H-a_q}{4}.
$$ 
Then, uniformly in \(x\in\mathbb R\), 
 \begin{align}
\int_\mathbb R G_r(x-y)^2\lambda(y)^{-2/q}\mathrm d y
\le  &\, C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}r^{-1/2},\label{t:eq:kernel-L2}\\ 
\int_{\mathbb R^2}|D_r(x-y,h)|^2|h|^{2H-2}|x-y|^{4\vartheta}\lambda(y)^{-2/q}\mathrm d y\mathrm d h
\le  &\, C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}r^{H+2\vartheta-1},\label{t:eq:kernel-weighted}\\
\int_\mathbb R |G_{r+\varepsilon}(x-y)-G_r(x-y)|^2\lambda(y)^{-2/q}\mathrm d y
\le  &\, C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}\varepsilon^2r^{-5/2},\label{t:eq:kernel-time-L2}\\
\int_{\mathbb R^2}|D_{r+\varepsilon}(x-y,h)-D_r(x-y,h)|^2|h|^{2H-2}\lambda(y)^{-2/q}\mathrm d y\mathrm d h
\le  &\, C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}\varepsilon^2r^{H-3}.\label{t:eq:kernel-time-H}
\end{align}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The scaling identities
\[
G_r(z)=r^{-1/2}G_1(z/\sqrt r),
\qquad
D_r(z,h)=r^{-1/2}D_1(z/\sqrt r,h/\sqrt r),
\]
together with the substitutions
$y=x-\sqrt r\,z$, $h=\sqrt r\,w$, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:initial-smoothing}(i), reduce
\eqref{t:eq:kernel-L2} and \eqref{t:eq:kernel-weighted}
to the finiteness of
\[
\int_\mathbb R G_1(z)^2(1+|z|)^{a_q}\mathrm d z
\]
and
\[
\int_{\mathbb R^2}
|D_1(z,w)|^2|w|^{2H-2}|z|^{4\vartheta}
(1+|z|)^{a_q}\mathrm d z\mathrm d w,
\]
respectively.
                                                   
                                                    
                     
The first integral is finite by Gaussian decay, while
Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz} yields
\[
\int_{\mathbb R^2}
|D_1(z,w)|^2|w|^{2H-2}|z|^{4\vartheta}
(1+|z|)^{a_q}\mathrm d z\mathrm d w
\le
C\int_\mathbb R
|z|^{4\vartheta}(1+|z|)^{a_q+2H-2}\mathrm d z<\infty,
\]
since $a_q+4\vartheta<1-2H$.

Since
\[
\partial_rG_r(z)
=
r^{-3/2}
\left(\frac{z^2}{4r}-\frac12\right)
G_1(z/\sqrt r),
\]
and $(w^2/4-1/2)G_1(w)$ is a Schwartz function,
the same scaling arguments give
\begin{align}
\int_\mathbb R|\partial_rG_r(x-y)|^2
\lambda(y)^{-2/q}\mathrm d y
&\le
C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}r^{-5/2},
\label{eq:derivative-temporal}\\
\int_{\mathbb R^2}
|\partial_rG_r(x+h-y)-\partial_rG_r(x-y)|^2
|h|^{2H-2}\lambda(y)^{-2/q}
\mathrm d h\mathrm d y
&\le
C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}r^{H-3}.
\label{eq:derivative-spatial}
\end{align}
Since $r\le T$ and $0<\varepsilon<1$, these estimates remain valid,
with a uniform constant, when $r$ is replaced by $r+s$
for $0\le s\le\varepsilon$. 


The identity
$$
G_{r+\varepsilon}-G_r
=
\int_0^\varepsilon \partial_sG_{r+s}\mathrm d s,
$$
together with Minkowski's inequality and
\eqref{eq:derivative-temporal}, gives 
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\int_\mathbb R
|G_{r+\varepsilon}(x-y)-G_r(x-y)|^2
\lambda(y)^{-2/q}\mathrm d y\\
\le&\,
\left(
\int_0^\varepsilon
\left(
\int_\mathbb R
|\partial_sG_{r+s}(x-y)|^2
\lambda(y)^{-2/q}\mathrm d y
\right)^{1/2}
\mathrm d s
\right)^2\\
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}
\left(
\int_0^\varepsilon(r+s)^{-5/4}\mathrm d s
\right)^2\\
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}\varepsilon^2r^{-5/2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Similarly,
\[
D_{r+\varepsilon}(x,h)-D_r(x,h)
=
\int_0^\varepsilon\partial_sD_{r+s}(x,h)\mathrm d s.
\]
Hence, by Minkowski's inequality and
\eqref{eq:derivative-spatial},
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\int_{\mathbb R^2}
|D_{r+\varepsilon}(x-y,h)-D_r(x-y,h)|^2
|h|^{2H-2}\lambda(y)^{-2/q}\mathrm d y\mathrm d h\\
\le&\,
\left(
\int_0^\varepsilon
\left(
\int_{\mathbb R^2}
|\partial_sD_{r+s}(x-y,h)|^2
|h|^{2H-2}\lambda(y)^{-2/q}
\mathrm d y\mathrm d h
\right)^{1/2}
\mathrm d s
\right)^2\\
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}
\left(
\int_0^\varepsilon(r+s)^{(H-3)/2}\mathrm d s
\right)^2\\
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}\varepsilon^2r^{H-3}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The proof is complete.

label: t:lem:integrated
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$, we may assume that
$\varepsilon^\beta<T$.

For (i), integrating \eqref{t:eq:kernel-time-H} over
$r\in[\varepsilon^\beta,T]$ gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\int_{\varepsilon^\beta}^T\int_{\mathbb R^2}
|D_{r+\varepsilon}(x-y,h)-D_r(x-y,h)|^2
|h|^{2H-2}\lambda(y)^{-2/q}\mathrm d y\mathrm d h\mathrm d r\\
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}\varepsilon^2
\int_{\varepsilon^\beta}^T r^{H-3}\mathrm d r\\
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}\varepsilon^{2+\beta(H-2)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

For (ii), split the integral over $(0,\varepsilon)$ and $(\varepsilon,T)$.
On $(0,\varepsilon)$, using \eqref{t:eq:kernel-L2} and
$$
|G_{r+\varepsilon}-G_r|^2
\le
2|G_{r+\varepsilon}|^2+2|G_r|^2,
$$
we obtain
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\int_0^\varepsilon\int_\mathbb R
|G_{r+\varepsilon}(x-y)-G_r(x-y)|^2
\lambda(y)^{-2/q}\mathrm d y\mathrm d r\\
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}
\int_0^\varepsilon
\bigl((r+\varepsilon)^{-1/2}+r^{-1/2}\bigr)\mathrm d r\\
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}\varepsilon^{1/2}.
\end{aligned}
$$
On $(\varepsilon,T)$, \eqref{t:eq:kernel-time-L2} gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
 \int_\varepsilon^T\int_\mathbb R
|G_{r+\varepsilon}(x-y)-G_r(x-y)|^2
\lambda(y)^{-2/q}\mathrm d y\mathrm d r 
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}\varepsilon^2
\int_\varepsilon^T r^{-5/2}\mathrm d r\\
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}\varepsilon^{1/2}.
\end{aligned}
$$
This proves \eqref{t:eq:integrated-L2}.

For (iii), \eqref{t:eq:kernel-weighted} yields
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\int_0^{\varepsilon^\beta}\int_{\mathbb R^2}
\bigl(
|D_r(x-y,h)|^2+
|D_{r+\varepsilon}(x-y,h)|^2
\bigr)
|h|^{2H-2}|x-y|^{4\vartheta}
\lambda(y)^{-2/q}\mathrm d y\mathrm d h\mathrm d r\\
\le&\,
C\lambda(x)^{-2/q}
\int_0^{\varepsilon^\beta}
\bigl(
r^{H+2\vartheta-1}
+(r+\varepsilon)^{H+2\vartheta-1}
\bigr)\mathrm d r.
\end{aligned}
$$
Using $\varepsilon\le\varepsilon^\beta$ and $H+2\vartheta>0$, we obtain
$$
\int_0^{\varepsilon^\beta}
\bigl(
r^{H+2\vartheta-1}
+(r+\varepsilon)^{H+2\vartheta-1}
\bigr)\mathrm d r
\le
C\varepsilon^{\beta(H+2\vartheta)}.
$$
Thus \eqref{t:eq:integrated-weighted} follows.

label: lem:energy
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{eq:inner},
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\int_0^\infty\int_{\mathbb R^2}
|D_r(z+h,\varepsilon)-D_r(z,\varepsilon)|^2
|h|^{2H-2}\mathrm d h\mathrm d z\mathrm d r\\
=&\,
\frac{c_{1,1}}{H(\frac12-H)}
\int_0^\infty\int_\mathbb R
|e^{i\varepsilon\xi}-1|^2e^{-2r\xi^2}
|\xi|^{1-2H}\mathrm d\xi\mathrm d r\\
=&\,
\frac{c_{1,1}}{2H(\frac12-H)}
\int_\mathbb R
|e^{i\varepsilon\xi}-1|^2|\xi|^{-1-2H}\mathrm d\xi\\
=&\,
\frac{c_{1,1}\varepsilon^{2H}}{2H(\frac12-H)}
\int_\mathbb R
|e^{iu}-1|^2|u|^{-1-2H}\mathrm d u\\
=&\,
\frac{\varepsilon^{2H}}{H(1-2H)}.
\end{aligned}
$$   Here we used the change of variables $u=\varepsilon\xi$ and the identity
$$
 \int_\mathbb R |e^{iu}-1|^2|u|^{-1-2H}\mathrm d u
 =\frac{2\pi}{\Gamma(2H+1)\sin(\pi H)}
 =c_{1,1}^{-1}.
$$

The proof is complete.

label: lem:tails
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq F-integ
title: Proof
body_md:
Lemma~\ref{lem:energy} with \(\varepsilon=1\) yields
\begin{align}\label{eq F-integ}
     \int_\mathbb R F_H(w)\mathrm d w<\infty.
\end{align}

We first show that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:FH-pointwise}
 F_H(w)\le C|w|^{2H-2},
 \qquad |w|>2.
\end{equation}
For \(0<s\le1\),
\[
 Q_H[D_s(\cdot,1)](w)
 \le 2Q_HG_s(w+1)+2Q_HG_s(w).
\]
By the scaling identity
\[
 Q_HG_s(w)
 =
 s^{H-3/2}Q_HG_1(w/\sqrt s)
\]
and Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz}, we obtain, for \(|w|>2\),
\[
 Q_H[D_s(\cdot,1)](w)
 \le C|w|^{2H-2}s^{-1/2}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \int_0^1 Q_H[D_s(\cdot,1)](w)\mathrm d s
 \le C|w|^{2H-2}.
\]


We also note the scaling relation
\begin{equation}\label{eq:heat-kernel-derivative-scaling}
G_s'(y)=s^{-1}G_1'(y/\sqrt{s}),
\qquad s>0,\ y\in\mathbb R.
\end{equation}
For $s\ge1$, we have
$$
D_s(\cdot,1)=\int_0^1G_s'(\cdot+v)\,\mathrm d v.
$$
Jensen's inequality, \eqref{eq:heat-kernel-derivative-scaling},
and Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz} therefore yield  
$$
Q_H[D_s(\cdot,1)](w)
\le
Cs^{H-5/2}
\left(1+\frac{|w|}{\sqrt{s}}\right)^{2H-2}.
$$
 
Hence, for \(|w|>2\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_1^\infty Q_H[D_s(\cdot,1)](w)\mathrm d s
\le &\, 
C|w|^{2H-2}
\int_1^{|w|^2/4}s^{-3/2}\mathrm d s
+
C\int_{|w|^2/4}^\infty s^{H-5/2}\mathrm d s\\
\le &\, 
C|w|^{2H-2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves \eqref{eq:FH-pointwise}.

For (i),  \eqref{eq F-integ} and
\eqref{eq:FH-pointwise} imply, for \(R>2\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{|w|\le R}|w|^{2\gamma}F_H(w)\mathrm d w
\le &\, 
C+
C\int_2^R r^{2\gamma+2H-2}\mathrm d r.
\end{aligned}
\]
The three cases in \eqref{eq:localmoment}  follow by considering whether
\(2\gamma+2H-1\) is positive, zero, or negative.
The case \(1\le R\le2\) follows directly from  \eqref{eq F-integ}.

For (ii), when \(R\ge2\),   by \eqref{eq:FH-pointwise} and \(a<1-2H\),  we have 
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{|w|>R}(1+|w|)^aF_H(w)\mathrm d w
\le &\, 
C\int_R^\infty r^{a+2H-2}\mathrm d r\\
\le &\, 
CR^{a+2H-1}.
\end{aligned}
\] 

The case $1\le R<2$ follows from \eqref{eq F-integ}
and the estimate above with $R=2$, after enlarging $C$.
This proves \eqref{eq:weightedtail}.

label: lem:weightedenergy
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:scaling
title: Proof
body_md:
With the change of variables
$$
r=\varepsilon^2s,\qquad z=\varepsilon w,\qquad h=\varepsilon\ell,
$$
the scaling of $D_r$ gives
$$
D_{\varepsilon^2s}(\varepsilon w+\varepsilon\ell,\varepsilon)-D_{\varepsilon^2s}(\varepsilon w,\varepsilon)
=
\varepsilon^{-1}\bigl[D_s(w+\ell,1)-D_s(w,1)\bigr].
$$
Hence, by Fubini's theorem, for every nonnegative measurable function $f$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:scaling}
\int_0^\infty\int_{\mathbb R^2}
|D_r(z+h,\varepsilon)-D_r(z,\varepsilon)|^2
|h|^{2H-2}f(z)\mathrm d h\mathrm d z\mathrm d r
=
\varepsilon^{2H}\int_\mathbb R F_H(w)f(\varepsilon w)\mathrm d w.
\end{equation}

Taking $f(z)=(1+|z|)^a$ in \eqref{eq:scaling} and using
$0<\varepsilon\le1$, we obtain
$$
\int_\mathbb R F_H(w)(1+\varepsilon|w|)^a\mathrm d w
\le
\int_\mathbb R F_H(w)(1+|w|)^a\mathrm d w.
$$
The integral on the right is finite: on $|w|\le1$ this follows from
$F_H\in L^1(\mathbb R)$, while on $|w|>1$ it follows from
\eqref{eq:weightedtail} with $R=1$. This proves
\eqref{eq:wenergy}.

For \eqref{eq:wlocalenergy}, take
$$
f(z)=(1+|z|)^a(|z|^{2\gamma}\wedge1)
$$
in \eqref{eq:scaling}, and write
$$
\varepsilon^{2H}\int_\mathbb R
F_H(w)(1+\varepsilon|w|)^a
(\varepsilon^{2\gamma}|w|^{2\gamma}\wedge1)\mathrm d w
=:J_1+J_2,
$$
where $J_1$ and $J_2$ are the integrals over
$|w|\le\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $|w|>\varepsilon^{-1}$, respectively.

For $J_1$,
$$
J_1
\le
C\varepsilon^{2H+2\gamma}
\int_{|w|\le\varepsilon^{-1}}
|w|^{2\gamma}F_H(w)\mathrm d w.
$$
Applying \eqref{eq:localmoment} with $R=\varepsilon^{-1}$ yields
$$
J_1\le
C
\begin{cases}
\varepsilon^{2H+2\gamma}+\varepsilon,
& 2\gamma+2H-1>0,\\
\varepsilon(1+|\log\varepsilon|),
& 2\gamma+2H-1=0,\\
\varepsilon^{2H+2\gamma},
& 2\gamma+2H-1<0.
\end{cases}
$$
 For $J_2$, since $|w|>\varepsilon^{-1}$,
$$
\varepsilon^{2\gamma}|w|^{2\gamma}\wedge1=1,
\qquad
(1+\varepsilon|w|)^a\le C\varepsilon^a(1+|w|)^a.
$$
Hence, by \eqref{eq:weightedtail},
$$
J_2
\le
C\varepsilon^{2H+a}
\int_{|w|>\varepsilon^{-1}}
(1+|w|)^aF_H(w)\mathrm d w
\le
C\varepsilon.
$$

Combining the estimates for $J_1$ and $J_2$ proves
\eqref{eq:wlocalenergy}.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:singleenergy}
\begin{itemize}

\item[(i)]
Let $0\le a<1$ and $0<\varepsilon\le1$. Then
$$
\int_0^\infty\int_\mathbb R
|D_r(z,\varepsilon)|^2(1+|z|)^a
\mathrm d z\mathrm d r
\le
C\varepsilon.
$$

\item[(ii)]
Let $b\ge0$, $0<\gamma<1$, $0<\rho\le1$, and
$0<\varepsilon\le\sqrt{\rho}$. Then
$$
\int_\mathbb R
|D_\rho(z,\varepsilon)|(1+|z|)^b
(|z|^\gamma\wedge1)\mathrm d z
\le
C\varepsilon\rho^{-(1-\gamma)/2}.
$$

\end{itemize}

title: Proof
body_md:
For (i), the scaling $r=\varepsilon^2s$ and $z=\varepsilon w$ gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
 \int_0^\infty\int_\mathbb R
|D_r(z,\varepsilon)|^2(1+|z|)^a\mathrm d z\mathrm d r
=&\,
\varepsilon\int_0^\infty\int_\mathbb R
|D_s(w,1)|^2(1+\varepsilon|w|)^a\mathrm d w\mathrm d s\\
\le&\,
\varepsilon\int_0^\infty\int_\mathbb R
|D_s(w,1)|^2(1+|w|)^a\mathrm d w\mathrm d s.
\end{aligned}
$$
It therefore suffices to show that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:single-energy-target}
\int_0^\infty\int_\mathbb R
|D_s(w,1)|^2(1+|w|)^a\mathrm d w\mathrm d s<\infty.
\end{equation}
For $0<s\le1$,
$$
|D_s(w,1)|^2
\le
2\bigl(G_s(w+1)^2+G_s(w)^2\bigr),
$$
and Gaussian decay yields
$$
\int_\mathbb R
|D_s(w,1)|^2(1+|w|)^a\mathrm d w
\le
Cs^{-1/2}.
$$
For $s\ge1$, using Jensen's inequality 
and  \eqref{eq:heat-kernel-derivative-scaling}, we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_\mathbb R|D_s(w,1)|^2(1+|w|)^a\mathrm d w
\le&\,
\int_0^1\int_\mathbb R
|G_s'(w+c)|^2(1+|w|)^a\mathrm d w\mathrm d c\\
\le&\,
Cs^{(a-3)/2}
\int_\mathbb R|G_1'(z)|^2(1+|z|)^a\mathrm d z\\
\le&\,
Cs^{(a-3)/2}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Since $a<1$, both bounds are integrable over their respective ranges,
which proves \eqref{eq:single-energy-target}.

For (ii), using $|z|^\gamma\wedge1\le|z|^\gamma$ and the
fundamental theorem of calculus, we obtain
$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_\mathbb R
|D_\rho(z,\varepsilon)|(1+|z|)^b(|z|^\gamma\wedge1)\mathrm d z
\le&\,
\varepsilon\int_0^1\int_\mathbb R
|G_\rho'(z+c\varepsilon)|(1+|z|)^b|z|^\gamma\mathrm d z\mathrm d c.
\end{aligned}
$$
Since $\varepsilon\le\sqrt{\rho}\le1$ and $0\le c\le1$,
$$
(1+|z|)^b\le C(1+|z+c\varepsilon|)^b,
\qquad
|z|^\gamma\le|z+c\varepsilon|^\gamma+\varepsilon^\gamma.
$$
Using the change of  variables $y=z+c\varepsilon$ and 
\eqref{eq:heat-kernel-derivative-scaling}, we obtain
$$
\begin{aligned}
 \int_\mathbb R
|D_\rho(z,\varepsilon)|(1+|z|)^b(|z|^\gamma\wedge1)\mathrm d z 
\le&\,
C\varepsilon\int_\mathbb R
|G_\rho'(y)|(1+|y|)^b
\bigl(|y|^\gamma+\varepsilon^\gamma\bigr)\mathrm d y\\
\le&\,
C\varepsilon\left(
\rho^{(\gamma-1)/2}
+\varepsilon^\gamma\rho^{-1/2}
\right)\\
\le&\,
C\varepsilon\rho^{-(1-\gamma)/2}.
\end{aligned}
$$ 

The proof is complete.
